objectives: Reason about query cost in cloud warehouses.

slides.title: Why columnar storage wins for analytics
slides.body:
OLTP databases (Postgres, MySQL) store data **row-oriented**: each row's columns are stored contiguously on disk. Fetch one row = one disk read. Optimal for transactional workloads (read 1 row, update it, write back).

Warehouses (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift, Databricks SQL) store data **column-oriented**: each column's values are stored contiguously. Fetch one row = one disk read per column (slow). But fetching ONE column across millions of rows = one contiguous scan (fast).

Analytics queries typically scan many rows but few columns ('SELECT revenue, country FROM sales WHERE year = 2024'). Column-store reads only the three needed columns; row-store would read every row's every column. The win at scale: 10-100× faster on typical analytical queries.

Bonus: columnar data compresses much better (similar values within a column compress well). Snowflake routinely achieves 5-10× compression vs raw CSV. Storage cost + I/O cost both drop substantially.

slides.title: Warehouse vs lake vs lakehouse
slides.body:
**Data warehouse** (Snowflake, BigQuery, Redshift): managed SQL engine + storage. Optimized for analytics. Strong SQL, decent ML support, expensive per-query compute.

**Data lake** (S3 + Parquet + Spark + Hive): raw files in object storage, queried by ad-hoc tools. Cheap storage, flexible (multiple engines can read the same files), but no built-in catalog, governance, or transactional updates.

**Lakehouse** (Delta Lake, Iceberg, Hudi): lake's storage flexibility + warehouse's transactional guarantees. Open-source table formats sitting on top of Parquet files in object storage. Provides ACID transactions, time travel, schema evolution. Databricks pushes Delta Lake; Snowflake / Iceberg / open standards are the alternative.

The industry is converging on the lakehouse pattern. Storage is open (Parquet + Iceberg/Delta); engines are interchangeable (Spark, Trino, Snowflake-on-Iceberg, DuckDB). The walled-garden warehouse (Snowflake's proprietary storage) gives ground each year to open lakehouse architectures.

question.question: A query `SELECT SUM(revenue) FROM sales WHERE year = 2024` on a 1TB table. Why does Snowflake (columnar) crush Postgres (row-store) on this query?
options: Snowflake scans only the `revenue` and `year` columns, not the dozen other columns; row-store reads every row's every column.
question.explanation: Columnar storage lets the engine scan only the columns needed for the query. For this query, that's `revenue` and `year` — maybe 5% of the table's volume. A row-store reads every row's every column (because rows are stored together) — 100% of the table's volume. At 1TB, that's 950GB of unnecessary disk I/O avoided by columnar. Compression (column-wise) further amplifies the win — typically 5-10× compression on real data.

hints: What fraction of the table does each storage layout actually read for this query?
Compare bytes read: column-store fetches only used columns; row-store fetches every column.
slides.workedSolution: Columnar storage stores values of the same column contiguously. The query reads only `revenue` + `year` (2 columns out of N). Row-store stores rows contiguously, so reading even just the values of two columns requires reading every full row (all columns). For 1TB data with 20 columns the column-store reads ~100GB; row-store reads 1TB. Plus columnar compresses 5-10× — making the effective scan even smaller.
